titleStmt.author: Marc Dierikx, Sacha Zala

msDesc.head: Reaktion der USA United States of America auf die Ereignisse in Berlin und der DDR seit dem 9.11.

msContents.summary: Die Reaktionen der US United States -Regierung, der Medien und der Öffentlichkeit auf die jüngsten Ereignisse in Berlin und der DDR werden dargestellt. Die eher verhaltene Erklärung von Präsident Bush, wird auf den Fokus der US United States -Regierung auf die Wahrung von Stabilität in der NATO North Atlantic Treaty Organization zurückführt.

Written by Gebhardt von Moltke and Eberhard Kölsch and signed by Gebhardt von Moltke and Frank Lambach. Seen on 16 November 1989 by Karl Heinz Kuhna and Dieter Kastrup, on 17 November 1989 by Jürgen Sudhoff and on 20 November 1989 by Hans-Dietrich Genscher. Also published in: Die Einheit. Das Auswärtige Amt, das DDR-Außenministerium und der Zwei-plus-Vier-Prozess, ed. by Horst Möller et. al. on behalf of the Institute for Contemporary History Munich–Berlin, Göttingen, 2015, doc. 22. for the Foreign Minister of the FRG Federal Republic of Germany , Hans-Dietrich Genscher
US United States Reaction to the Events in Berlin and the GDR German Democratic Republic since 9 November

div.p: For information (ahead of the forthcoming talks in WashingtonHans-Dietrich Genscher held talks in Washington on 20 and 21 November 1989.)

1. The events in Berlin and the GDR German Democratic Republic have dominated the US United States media for days. Interest in Germany and German/European- US United States relations has increased enormously among the public (top TV Television journalists have been sent to Berlin; evening news programmes have been broadcast in front of the Wall, with clips of historic scenes; there have been special features in the “Washington Post” and “New York Times” and Ambassador Ruhfus has given several TV Television interviews). Moving scenes (cheering, joy, spontaneous celebrations) and highly symbolic images (the Wall, Brandenburg Gate, people embracing and shedding tears of joy) reflect Americans’ tendency to be emotional and preference for images. A large wave of sympathy has gripped the entire country. This is of great help to our public diplomacy work and we should certainly make use of it. The Embassy and German Information Centres are working flat out to do so. The large number of requests for interviews provides a unique opportunity for Federal Government officials to present Germany and its policies to a broad and receptive US United States audience.

2. The resounding echo in the media and among the US United States public made the Administration’s reaction, which largely reflects our own, look rather subdued in contrast. The focus is on realism, safeguarding stability and, most importantly, preserving unity in NATO North Atlantic Treaty Organization . On the evening of 9 November, Bush said (in Baker’s presence and with no expression on his face) that he was “very pleased” about the opening of the GDR German Democratic Republic
borders. He praised the Federal Government for having “done a magnificent job”, but was reserved about further developments and said it was “way too early” to speak about reunification. Asked why he did not seem to be “elated”, Bush said he was “just not an emotional kind of guy”.

On the following day, Baker said he was “extremely happy”; however, in interviews he described an implied connection between the events and reunification as “premature” (10.11.1989 MacNeil/LehrerThe US United States journalists Robert MacNeil (*1931) and Jim Lehrer (*1934), hosted The MacNeil/Lehrer NewsHour on the TV Television channel PBS.). For his part, Vice-President Quayle has said that “the reunification of Germany is inevitable”.
There are three reasons for Bush and Baker’s cautious statements:

– the desire to signal to the Soviet Union in the run-up to the summit near Malta that the US United States does not wish to see the stability of developments in Central and East Europe and Gorbachev’s position in light of critics of his reform process endangered by thoughtless expressions of feelings of triumph. Bush and Baker are thus interpreting Gorbachev’s concerns correctly (cf. Gorbachev’s message to Bush on the night of 10/11 November, in which he said that he was “very concerned about the possibility of destabilisation”; similar reaction by Ambassador Kotchemassov in a meeting with Ambassador Walters in East Berlin on 11 November.) Referring explicitly to your telephone call (10 November), Baker underlined that the development in the GDR German Democratic Republic was also an achievement resulting from the united stance shown by the US United States and NATO North Atlantic Treaty Organization
(10.11. MacNeil/Lehrer, 12.11. BrinkleyThe US United States journalist David Brinkley (1920–2003), hosted the news broadcast This Week on the TV Television channel ABC.). Secretary of Defence Cheney reacted in a similar, but more forceful way;

– concern that a more emphatic reaction would inevitably lead to the question of practical measures to support reform in the GDR German Democratic Republic , with financial implications – and at a time when the Administration was being criticised for not providing enough financial support for the reform process in Poland and Hungary.
– Bush and Baker’s characters and governing style based on a case-by-case approach to crisis management, which deliberately refrains from using far-reaching concepts.

The summit with Gorbachev on 2 and 3 December has become even more relevant on account of the events in the GDR German Democratic Republic . The Administration is doing everything it can to counteract the impression that it wants to make decisions over the allies’ heads at this summit on far-reaching arrangements on a postwar order in Central Europe. On the other hand, Bush’s and Baker’s reactions, as far as we have seen so far, merely hint that the West already has a concept for a European peace order and proven instruments for West East dialogue in the form of the Harmel Report
Report of the Council on the Future Tasks of the Alliance (Harmel Report) of 13 and 14 December 1967, https://www.nato.int/cps/en/natohq/topics_67927.htm. and the
CSCE Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe process.
